nodes.label: Sequences, Series and Progressions
nodes.note: Sequences and series underpin JEE algebra: AP, GP, HP, arithmetico-geometric series, and telescoping methods. Expect one question every year built on nth-term and sum identities.

nodes.label: Sequence Fundamentals
nodes.note: Definitions and core invariants that link a sequence to its partial sums. These identities are the entry point for almost every JEE series problem.

nodes.label: Sequence as a Function
nodes.note: A sequence assigns each natural number n a unique term: $$a_n = f(n), \ n \in \mathbb{N}$$. Finite and infinite types both appear in sum-of-n problems.

nodes.label: Series and Partial Sums
nodes.note: A series is the indicated sum of terms, and its partial sum is $$S_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k$$. JEE problems often hand you S_n and ask for the sum of specific terms.

nodes.label: Term from Sum Relation
nodes.note: Recover the nth term from the partial sums: $$a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \ (n \ge 2), \ a_1 = S_1$$. The n >= 2 restriction is a classic off-by-one trap.

nodes.label: Mini-Example: S_n Given
nodes.note: If $S_n = 2n^2 + 3n$, then $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} = 4n + 1$ for $n \ge 2$, and $a_1 = S_1 = 5$, which matches $4(1)+1$.

nodes.label: Finite vs Infinite Sums
nodes.note: Finite series stop at a last term, while infinite series need a convergence check before any sum formula applies. $$S_\infty = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k$$ exists only when terms vanish fast enough.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Progression
nodes.note: The workhorse of JEE sequences: constant difference between consecutive terms. Most questions reduce to the nth-term or sum formula.

nodes.label: Common Difference
nodes.note: The difference is constant: $$d = a_{k+1} - a_k$$. A zero d gives a constant sequence, worth spotting in modified progressions.

nodes.label: nth Term of an AP
nodes.note: The general term is $$T_n = a + (n-1)d$$. Asking which term equals X is a direct linear equation in n.

nodes.label: Sum of n Terms of AP
nodes.note: The sum of the first n terms is $$S_n = \frac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n-1)d\right]$$. It is quadratic in n, so a quadratic S_n signals an AP.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Mean
nodes.note: The middle term of three terms in AP is their mean: $$b = \frac{a+c}{2}$$. Inserting k AMs between a and b is a standard JEE step.

nodes.label: Equidistant Term Property
nodes.note: Terms equidistant from the ends sum equally: $$a_k + a_{n+1-k} = a_1 + a_n$$. Use it to shortcut sums of symmetric selected terms.

nodes.label: Example: Sum of an AP
nodes.note: For $3, 7, 11, \dots$ ($a=3, d=4$): $S_{20} = \frac{20}{2}[6 + 19\cdot 4] = 820$. JEE wraps this in word problems about arithmetic totals.

nodes.label: Geometric Progression
nodes.note: Constant ratio between consecutive terms. Infinite GP sums and mean relations are heavily tested.

nodes.label: Common Ratio
nodes.note: Each term is a fixed multiple of the previous: $$r = \frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}$$. The sign and magnitude of r decide monotonicity and convergence.

nodes.label: nth Term of a GP
nodes.note: The general term is $$T_n = ar^{n-1}$$. Logarithms convert GP problems into AP problems, a standard JEE manipulation.

nodes.label: Sum of n Terms of GP
nodes.note: For r not equal to 1 the partial sum is $$S_n = a\frac{r^n - 1}{r - 1}$$. The $r = 1$ case collapses to $S_n = na$.

nodes.label: Infinite Geometric Sum
nodes.note: When $|r| < 1$ the series converges: $$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r}$$. This single formula powers recurring-decimal and geometric-tail questions.

nodes.label: Geometric Mean
nodes.note: For three terms in GP, the middle is the geometric mean: $$b^2 = ac$$. Two positive numbers have GM $\sqrt{ac}$, linking to the AM-GM-HM chain.

nodes.label: Harmonic Progression
nodes.note: Reciprocals form an AP. HP questions are usually disguised AM/GM problems.

nodes.label: HP Definition
nodes.note: A sequence is harmonic when its reciprocals form an AP: $$\frac{1}{a_{k+1}} - \frac{1}{a_k} = \text{constant}$$. Its nth term mirrors the AP structure on reciprocals.

nodes.label: nth Term of an HP
nodes.note: If reciprocals are an AP with first A and difference D, then $$T_n = \frac{1}{A + (n-1)D}$$. Take reciprocals first, then apply AP formulas.

nodes.label: Harmonic Mean
nodes.note: The harmonic mean of two numbers is $$H = \frac{2ab}{a+b}$$. HM of a and b is the reciprocal of the AM of $1/a$ and $1/b$.

nodes.label: Example: HM of Two Numbers
nodes.note: HM of 2 and 6 is $H = \frac{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 6}{2 + 6} = 3$, and $2, 3, 6$ are in HP since $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{6}$ are in AP.

nodes.label: Means and Inequalities
nodes.note: AM-GM-HM relations and Cauchy-Schwarz give quick answers to max-min JEE questions.

nodes.label: AM-GM-HM Chain
nodes.note: For positive reals the three means are ordered: $$AM \ge GM \ge HM$$. Equality holds iff all numbers are equal.

nodes.label: Weighted AM-GM
nodes.note: Weights turn the inequality into $$w_1 a_1 + w_2 a_2 \ge a_1^{w_1} a_2^{w_2}, \ w_1 + w_2 = 1$$. Handy for optimization under a constraint.

nodes.label: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
nodes.note: $$(a_1^2 + a_2^2)(b_1^2 + b_2^2) \ge (a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2)^2$$ bounds a dot product by the product of norms. Common in sum-bound questions.

nodes.label: Example: Max Product
nodes.note: For $x + y = 10$, AM-GM gives $\sqrt{xy} \le 5$, so the product $xy \le 25$, maximized at $x = y = 5$.

nodes.label: Arithmetico-Geometric Progression
nodes.note: Product of an AP and a GP term by term. The shift-and-subtract derivation is the key skill.

nodes.label: AGP Term Structure
nodes.note: Each term multiplies an AP factor by a GP factor: $$T_n = [a + (n-1)d]\, r^{n-1}$$. Recognize the mixed structure before applying formulas.

nodes.label: AGP Finite Sum
nodes.note: Multiply $S_n$ by r and subtract to collapse the series: $$S_n = \frac{a - [a+(n-1)d]r^n}{1-r} + \frac{dr(1 - r^{n-1})}{(1-r)^2}$$. The shift-and-subtract idea is asked conceptually in JEE.

nodes.label: AGP Infinite Sum
nodes.note: For $|r| < 1$: $$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r} + \frac{dr}{(1-r)^2}$$. The second term is the correction from the arithmetic part.

nodes.label: Example: 2 + 8 + 24 + 64
nodes.note: For $S = 1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot 4 + 3\cdot 8 + \dots$ the AGP has $a=1, d=1, r=2$; since $|r|>1$ only finite partial sums exist, found via shift-and-subtract.

nodes.label: Summation Methods
nodes.note: Difference tables, telescoping, and sigma identities cover non-standard series in JEE.

nodes.label: Method of Differences
nodes.note: Successive differences reveal the polynomial degree of the nth term: $$\Delta T_n = T_{n+1} - T_n$$. If the first differences are constant, T_n is linear; two rounds give a quadratic.

nodes.label: Telescoping Series
nodes.note: Write each term as a difference and cancel in between: $$\sum_{k=1}^{n}(V_k - V_{k-1}) = V_n - V_0$$. Partial-fraction splits set this up.

nodes.label: Example: Telescoping Sum
nodes.note: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \sum \left(\frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k+1}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1}$, a classic telescoping collapse.

nodes.label: Standard Sigma Identities
nodes.note: $$\sum_{k=1}^n k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \quad \sum_{k=1}^n k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}, \quad \sum_{k=1}^n k^3 = \left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$$. Memorize all three for direct use.
